title_original: The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party
editorial_title_zh: Hyperallergic 万圣节派对的最佳艺术造型
editorial_excerpt_zh: 从《两幅弗里达》到行走的伊娃·海瑟雕塑，Hyperallergic 的成员、读者、朋友和艺术家们为我们的第二届年度变装大赛带来了节日精神。

"一个荷兰静物画、“野兽耶稣”、几个深奥的戈雅角色，以及不仅一个而是两个玛丽娜·阿布拉莫维奇/乌雷的典故（甚至还不是最显而易见的那些！）走进了一家酒吧……这就是 Hyperallergic 的万圣节，宝贝！", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "10月28日星期三晚上，近200名我们的成员、读者、艺术家、支持者以及他们热情的朋友齐聚布鲁克林的奥伯伦（Oberon），参加我们一年一度的艺术造型派对。从“全场最佳”到“最有可能在佛罗里达州被禁”等多个类别的获奖者们展现了他们内心的艺术史书呆子魂，既化身成了立刻就能认出的标志性形象——罗伊·利希滕斯坦的《沉溺的女孩》和约翰内斯·维米尔的《戴珍珠耳环的少女》——也化身成了令人赞叹的冷门典故（哦，原来她是一个伊娃·海瑟的绳索雕塑？！）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们非常感谢我们聪明得离谱、充满创意和手艺精湛的社群对这个节日的投入。特别要感谢扎克·汤普森（Zac Thompson）拍摄的精彩照片，这些照片将帮助我们在未来的许多日子里重温这个夜晚，或者至少在我们急不可耐地等待明年到来之际……🌝", "links": [{"text": "Zac article_text:
Features

The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party

From “Las Dos Fridas” to a walking Eva Hesse sculpture, Hyperallergic members, readers, friends, and artists brought the spirit of the season to our second annual costume contest.

Hyperallergic )

A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... That’s a Hyperallergic Halloween, baby!

On Wednesday evening, October 28, almost 200 of our members, readers, artists, supporters, and their enthusiastic friends rolled into Oberon in Brooklyn for our annual art costume party. Winners in several categories ranging from “Best in Show” to “Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida” brought out the art-history nerd within them, materializing into both immediately recognizable icons — Roy Lichtenstein's “Drowning Girls” and Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” — and admirably obscure references ( oh, she was an Eva Hesse rope sculpture?! ).

We’re so grateful to our absurdly smart, creative, and crafty community for their commitment to the bit. And a big shout-out to Zac Thompson for their incredible photographs, which will help us relive the night for many moons, or at least as we wait impatiently for next year ... 🌝

Best in Show

Best in Show winners Emilio Rojas and Chico Raro as Pedro Lemebel and Francisco Casa Silva of Las Yeguas del Apocalipsis’s “ Las Dos Fridas ” (1989). No bribing was necessary to convince the panel.

Most Esoteric

Zoë Lescaze and Michael Rossi made every part of their costumes from scratch — yes, including the chair — to dress as lesser-known characters from Francisco Goya's Los caprichos (1797–98) series. The couple was among the winners of the "Most Esoteric" award, naturally.

Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida

Richard Prince's "Wayward Nurse" (2005), part of the artist's series critiquing the sexualization of nurses on pulp-fiction book covers, would not fly in the Sunshine State in 2026!

Most Likely to Get Acquired by a Museum Unironically

Curators and staff from the Heckscher Museum of Art in Huntington, New York, recreated a painting from the institution's own collection: George Grosz's antifascist "Eclipse of the Sun" (1926).

People's Choice

Melissa Brown and Marie Lorenz won over the crowd as none other than the infamously botched “Ecce Homo” aka “ Beast Jesus ” and its author, restorer Cecilia Giménez Zueco!

Hyperallergic Co-founders Veken Gueyikian and Hrag Vartanian with one of this year's costume contest judges, Nicholas D. Lowry, president of Swann Auction Galleries. Veken is Kazimir Malevich’s “Black Square” (1915), and Vartanian is a 17th-century Dutch still life painting — check out the skull! ( Memento mori , very Halloween-coded.)

Our wonderful costume contest judges! Left to right: New York Democratic Congressional candidate Claire Valdez , artist Jia Sung as the Spirit of Spirit Airlines (aka what everyone used to take to get to Art Basel Miami Beach), critic Aruna D’Souza in sleek black feathers, and Nicholas D. Lowry as a fashionable pumpkin in plaid.

Hyperallergic Staff Writer Anna Lee as Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (c. 1665) — an art-history classic, made otherworldly by photographer Zac Thompson’s expert double exposure.

These guests brought Museo del Prado right to your doorstep as a rather gory version of Francisco Goya's “Saturn Devouring His Son” (1820–23). Body horror !

Artist Coco Fusco donned one of the fabulous works in Marisol's wearable wooden sculpture "Three Women with Umbrella" (1965–66). Who says Pop art is dead?

If we had a “Cutest” category this year, this pawesome group would have taken the gold! Left to right: Will Swanson, Dwai, Cosette Patterson, Lauren Blaser, Shelby Roller, Sophia Tedesco, and Daniela Alonso as Cassius Marcellus Coolidge’s “ A Friend in Need ” (1903).

Emily Dotsikas of Alma Communications as Roy Lichtenstein’s “Drawing Girl” (1963). Brad, who?

Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara addresses the crowd after a very competitive contest. Just don't ask him what his costume is!

Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Rest Energy” (1980). There’s nothing scarier than a multi-year situationship, except maybe literally putting your heart in the hands of your lover.

Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar went as Snoopy for the fourth year in a row, a costume she calls her “magnum opus.”

“I made this Snoopy costume with stuff that I already had at home — the ears, spot, and tail were from an old black tee; I painted an old beauty blender black and used it as Snoopy's nose,” Nayyar shared. “My love of this cartoon beagle is well-known and documented . I'm already a crazy dog lady, but there's something about Snoopy's cheeky attitude and ridiculous antics that flips the script on the ‘man's best friend’ marker, which I find really liberating and inspirational.”

Writer Clara Maria Apostolatos (right) and her partner joined forces, quite literally, to embody Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Relation in Time” (1977).

What still life is complete without its peckish butterfly? Houry Geudelekian and Hyperallergic Co-founder and Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian make a perfect pair.

Us: “What are you?” Artist Danielle De Jesus: “I'm a broke MFA student!”

Just brilliant, down to the Whitney Museum artist lifetime pass!

Hyperallergic contributors Julie Schneider (middle) as a Keith Haring subway drawing and Daniela Mayer (far right) as an AI girlfriend, with Felix Moody as water and Brian Henderson as Candy Warhol (not pictured: candy corn costume).

Artists Jesse Lambert as Ray Johnson and Linda Ganjian as Eva Hesse's rope sculpture "No title" (1970). Is this what they mean by a two-person show?

Writer Jennifer Samet of Hyperallergic 's beloved “ Beer With a Painter ” column arrived as the ultimate tastemaker: Peggy Guggenheim.

Cheryl Hageman, deputy director of MTA Arts & Design, as a painting from Georgia O'Keeffe's Sky Above Clouds (1960–77) series.

excerpt_original: From “Las Dos Fridas” to a walking Eva Hesse sculpture, Hyperallergic members, readers, friends, and artists brought the spirit of the season to our second annual costume contest.

title_original: 【関西プレビュー】「Timeless Code　現代⇔江戸」福田美術館で27年1月30日から 江戸絵画の名作と現代作家による作品約70点が時を超えて競演
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0acba9e6574554b9b0032c8bcdbebcf9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "奈良美智《Are You Staying True to You?》 1997年　福田美術館蔵　通期展示　©YOSHITOMO NARA", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "福田美術館（京都市右京区）で、「Timeless Code 現代⇔江戸」が2027年1月30日から開催されます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同館では、これまで近世や近代の日本画を中心に、誰もがアートに親しめるような展覧会が開催されてきました。一方で近年、日本人の現代アーティストの活動が世界で高く評価され、世界中に強い影響を与えてきました。先般、惜しまれつつこの世を去った草間彌生（1929-2026）をはじめ、奈良美智（1959-）らの足跡をたどる大規模な回顧展も国内外で増えています。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "そこで福田美術館でも、近世から現代に至る日本美術の流れをたどり、その変遷の一端に触れる機会を創出するべく、2023年から日本人アーティストによる現代アートの蒐集が始まっています。2025年11月には、「現代アートコレクション第1弾」として、世界的に高い評価を受けているアーティストである奈良美智と加藤泉（1969-）の立体作品2作品が庭園内に設置されました。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展で焦点が当てられるのは、「現代」と「江戸時代」、それぞれを代表する作家たちです。会場では、時代の先駆者として世界を魅了し続けた草間彌生や、奈良美智、加藤泉ら海外でも活躍する現代アーティストの作品と、伊藤若冲（1716-1800）、池大雅（1723-1776）、円山応挙（1733-1795）ら江戸時代の巨匠の作品を比較できるように展示。時代や社会という枠組みを超えて共通する、創作に対する信念や表現方法が浮き彫りにされます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "さらに、夫婦で世界へと活躍の場を広げ、大きな注目を集めている西村有（1982-）と今井麗（1982-）の作品も紹介されます。現代アートと江戸絵画。およそ200年の時を超えて出会う作家たちが展示室で共鳴します。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "第1章では、奈良美智が愛知県立芸術大学大学院に在学中だった27歳から40代前半の作品が主に展示されます。また、奈良美智の作品と江戸時代の画家・池大雅や長沢芦雪の作品と相対して見せる試みも見どころです。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "奈良美智《UKIYO》は、江戸時代の浮世絵を背景や借景にして少女などのキャラクターを描き加えた、1999年制作の代表的な版画・コピー作品です。本展では《UKIYO》シリーズから9点が展示されます。また、2002年に制作されたアクリル画《真夜中のネコ型ロボット》（藤子プロ）は、美術館での展示機会が大変少ない、貴重な作品です。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "奈良美智が描く人物には特定のモデルがなく、「すべて自画像のようなもの」だと述べています。彼は学生時代の欧州旅行や1988から1999年のドイツ滞在を経て、言葉の通じない環境で自己の内面を深く見つめ直しました。一方、江戸時代の池大雅も、三度の富士登山や全国を遊歴した経験を持つ画家です。大雅にとっての旅は、「万巻の書を読み、万里の路を行く」という文人画の理念を日本で体現する、真摯な精神の研鑽でした。両者は国や時代こそ違えど、旅を己の表現の拠って立つ場所だったと考えられます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「キャンバスは鏡のようなもので、そこに写る自分をなぞっていく」と語る奈良の自画像。そして、実際の自然に触れた経験と高い学識から、独自の境地を完成させた大雅の山水図は、いずれも時空を超えて画面の上に立ち現れた、作家自身の精神そのものに他なりません。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "草間彌生と伊藤若冲の絵画は、細部への異常なまでのこだわりと、モチーフを繰り返し描く反復の技法において深く共鳴しています。1929年に生まれた草間彌生は、1940年代後半から制作活動をスタートさせました。「赤や緑や黄の水玉模様は、地球のマルでも、太陽のマルでも、月のマルでも、何でもいい。形式や意味づけはどうでもいいのである。人体に水玉模様を描くことによって、その人は自己を消滅し、宇宙の自然に帰る、というのが私の主張なのである。」（草間彌生『無限の網』 作品社、2002年）と語る草間は、同じモチーフの連続によって画面を埋め尽くしました。彼女の描く無数の水玉や網目は、無限に増殖しながら、個の境界を消し去るゼロ空間を生み出しています。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第2章では、1950年代の初期作品から2010年代の作品まで、草間彌生の絵画作品5点を鳥や神獣を描いた若冲作品と対比させながら紹介されます。（※出品作品・点数は変更される場合があります。）"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
福田美術館（京都市右京区）で、「Timeless Code 現代⇔江戸」が2027年1月30日から開催されます。

同館では、これまで近世や近代の日本画を中心に、誰もがアートに親しめるような展覧会が開催されてきました。一方で近年、日本人の現代アーティストの活動が世界で高く評価され、世界中に強い影響を与えてきました。先般、惜しまれつつこの世を去った草間彌生（1929-2026）をはじめ、奈良美智（1959-）らの足跡をたどる大規模な回顧展も国内外で増えています。

そこで福田美術館でも、近世から現代に至る日本美術の流れをたどり、その変遷の一端に触れる機会を創出するべく、2023年から日本人アーティストによる現代アートの蒐集が始まっています。2025年11月には、「現代アートコレクション第1弾」として、世界的に高い評価を受けているアーティストである奈良美智と加藤泉（1969-）の立体作品2作品が庭園内に設置されました。

本展で焦点が当てられるのは、「現代」と「江戸時代」、それぞれを代表する作家たちです。会場では、時代の先駆者として世界を魅了し続けた草間彌生や、奈良美智、加藤泉ら海外でも活躍する現代アーティストの作品と、伊藤若冲（1716-1800）、池大雅（1723-1776）、円山応挙（1733-1795）ら江戸時代の巨匠の作品を比較できるように展示。時代や社会という枠組みを超えて共通する、創作に対する信念や表現方法が浮き彫りにされます。

さらに、夫婦で世界へと活躍の場を広げ、大きな注目を集めている西村有（1982-）と今井麗（1982-）の作品も紹介されます。現代アートと江戸絵画。およそ200年の時を超えて出会う作家たちが展示室で共鳴します。

Timeless Code 現代⇔江戸

会場：福田美術館（京都府京都市右京区嵯峨天龍寺芒ノ馬場町3-16）

会期：2027年1月30日（土）～6月6日（日） ［前期：1/30～4/5、後期：4/6～6/6］

開館時間：10:00～17:00（最終入館16:30）

休館日：2/9（火）、3/2（火）、4/13（火）、5/18（火）

料金：一般 1,600円、高校生 1,000円、小・中学生 600円 ※障がい者と介添人1名まで各1,000円、幼児無料

アクセス： JR山陰本線（嵯峨野線）「嵯峨嵐山駅」下車徒歩12分 阪急嵐山線「嵐山駅」下車徒歩11分 嵐電（京福電鉄）「嵐山駅」下車徒歩4分

詳細は、 福田美術館公式サイト まで。

第1章 内なる象（かたち） 奈良美智⇔江戸

時空を超えて表される奈良美智と池大雅の精神世界

第1章では、奈良美智が愛知県立芸術大学大学院に在学中だった27歳から40代前半の作品が主に展示されます。また、奈良美智の作品と江戸時代の画家・池大雅や長沢芦雪の作品と相対して見せる試みも見どころです。

奈良美智《UKIYO》は、江戸時代の浮世絵を背景や借景にして少女などのキャラクターを描き加えた、1999年制作の代表的な版画・コピー作品です。本展では《UKIYO》シリーズから9点が展示されます。また、2002年に制作されたアクリル画《真夜中のネコ型ロボット》（藤子プロ）は、美術館での展示機会が大変少ない、貴重な作品です。

奈良美智が描く人物には特定のモデルがなく、「すべて自画像のようなもの」だと述べています。彼は学生時代の欧州旅行や1988から1999年のドイツ滞在を経て、言葉の通じない環境で自己の内面を深く見つめ直しました。一方、江戸時代の池大雅も、三度の富士登山や全国を遊歴した経験を持つ画家です。大雅にとっての旅は、「万巻の書を読み、万里の路を行く」という文人画の理念を日本で体現する、真摯な精神の研鑽でした。両者は国や時代こそ違えど、旅を己の表現の拠って立つ場所だったと考えられます。

「キャンバスは鏡のようなもので、そこに写る自分をなぞっていく」と語る奈良の自画像。そして、実際の自然に触れた経験と高い学識から、独自の境地を完成させた大雅の山水図は、いずれも時空を超えて画面の上に立ち現れた、作家自身の精神そのものに他なりません。

第2章 草間彌生⇔伊藤若冲

緻密な表現と反復の美から見出す、草間彌生と若冲の命の輝き

草間彌生と伊藤若冲の絵画は、細部への異常なまでのこだわりと、モチーフを繰り返し描く反復の技法において深く共鳴しています。1929年に生まれた草間彌生は、1940年代後半から制作活動をスタートさせました。「赤や緑や黄の水玉模様は、地球のマルでも、太陽のマルでも、月のマルでも、何でもいい。形式や意味づけはどうでもいいのである。人体に水玉模様を描くことによって、その人は自己を消滅し、宇宙の自然に帰る、というのが私の主張なのである。」（草間彌生『無限の網』 作品社、2002年）と語る草間は、同じモチーフの連続によって画面を埋め尽くしました。彼女の描く無数の水玉や網目は、無限に増殖しながら、個の境界を消し去るゼロ空間を生み出しています。

第2章では、1950年代の初期作品から2010年代の作品まで、草間彌生の絵画作品5点を鳥や神獣を描いた若冲作品と対比させながら紹介されます。（※出品作品・点数は変更される場合があります。）

江戸時代に活躍した若冲もまた、庭の鶏を徹底的に観察し、その姿を繰り返し描き続けた絵師です。個々の羽毛は驚くほど緻密に描き込まれていながらも、鶏の姿全体として生き生きとした躍動感に満ちています。

細部を極限まで突き詰める両者の姿勢は、単なる写実や装飾の域をはるかに超えるものです。二人が紡ぎ出す画面は、部分と全体の境界を溶かし、命の輝きを私たちに見せてくれます。

第3章 加藤泉⇔江戸

加藤泉の初公開作品にも注目。心の揺らぎを生み出す「カタチ」

美術における「形」は、見る人の感情を理屈抜きに揺さぶる力を持っています。

加藤泉はどこかミステリアスな「人がた」の絵画を生み出してきました。その独自の造形を前にするとき、そこに広がるのは、言葉では捉えきれない世界です。観る者は、相反する「不気味さ」と「懐かしさ」が入り混じる、本能的な感情の揺らぎを体験することになるでしょう。

第3章では、加藤泉の立体作品5点、本展で初公開予定の作品1点を含む平面作品10点を展示します。立体作品では、加藤がコロナ禍で制作を進めたヴィンテージのプラモデルと木彫などの「人がた」を合体させた立体作品シリーズ3点のほか、創業470周年を迎えた京友禅の老舗「千總」とコラボレーションして2024年に制作した着物《無題》などを紹介されます。同作は、加藤によるスケッチをもとに、絞りや刺繍など京友禅で受け継がれてきた様々な技術を用いて制作された、タイムレスな魅力を感じさせる作品です。

加藤泉の作品と共に展示されるのは、江戸時代の禅僧で、日本臨済禅中興の祖とされる 白隠慧鶴 （1685-1768）の作品です。白隠は、禅の教えを広めるために型破りでインパクトのある禅画や書を描き、民衆に教えを説きました。人間が抱える悩みや苦しみは、人によって全く異なります。見る人は自分の状況に当てはめて、自由なメッセージを受け取ることができるのです。両者が描く「カタチ」は、鑑賞者の精神へストレートに作用し、多様な心の揺らぎを生み出します。

第4章 響き合う二つの世界：西村有と今井麗

世界が注目する現代美術家の夫婦が織りなす、異なる二つの世界の共鳴

第4章では、多摩美術大学の同級生であり、現在は夫婦として共に世界を舞台に活躍を続ける二人の現代美術家、 西村有 （1982-）と 今井麗 （1982-）の作品を同時に展示します。

日常の何気ない風景や人々の気配を、軽やかな筆致と重層的な色面で描き出す西村有。それに対し、食卓のトーストや果物、お気に入りのぬいぐるみなど、身近な静物たちを古典的な油彩技法と鮮烈な光の描写で捉える今井麗。表現手法や画風、選ぶモチーフは一見すると全く異なります。しかし、同じ時間を共有し、同じ時代を駆け抜けてきた二人の作品の間には、不思議な調和と、お互いへのリスペクトが満ちているようです。

それぞれの歩みが交差し、響き合う二人の世界が紹介されます。

約200年という時空の隔たりを超えて、江戸絵画の巨匠たちと現代を牽引するトップアーティストたちが同じ空間で対峙する本展。緻密な反復のなかに生命の輝きを宿す若冲と草間彌生、旅や自己の内省を通じて魂の境地を画面に立ち現せる池大雅と奈良美智、見る者の本能的な感情を揺さぶる白隠慧鶴と加藤泉の力強い造形など、意外性と驚きに満ちた対比展示が非常に楽しみです。さらには新出作品の初公開や、今まさに熱い視線を集める西村有・今井麗夫妻の競演など、見どころは尽きません。福田美術館の洗練された展示空間で、時代を超越した美のコードがどのように響き合うのか、ぜひじっくりと体感してみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

Guide

12 Must-Read Books on Textiles and Fiber Art

Titles on contemporary Diné weavers, Black American quilting in California, the Bayeux Tapestry, artists including Cecilia Vicuña and Olga de Amaral, and more.

Hyperallergic )

There’s a reason the lexicon of textiles and fiber lends itself so well to storytelling — we thread the needle, weave the tale, spin the yarn. Writers have reached for these metaphors for centuries because they feel true to life, but artists know they’re also true to craft and its tangled histories. We’ve gathered a few recent books on embroidery, fiber art, weaving, and more that deserve a closer look, from Black Southern quilting and Korean bojagi to Palestinian tatreez and contemporary Diné weaving. Refreshingly, so many of these titles complicate or refuse reductive, familiar frameworks and open up new ways to understand the meditative and political dimensions of textile traditions, moving past the false dichotomy of “craft versus art” and sexist and tired notions of “women’s work.” You might even say these books piece together a new history of textile art, stitch by stitch. — Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

Reparative Craft: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick as a Textile Artist by Jason Edwards | Duke University Press, 2026

I know Eve Sedgwick from her deeply influential work in queer and literary theory, but it had somehow escaped me that she was also an artist. This book, which straddles literary and craft theory, examines her textile art between the mid-1990s and 2000s — the period in which she was also writing Touching Feeling . Some of those same ideas — particularly her preoccupation with Buddhism — can be found in her dreamy textile collages and sculptures meditating on illness, repair, and death. — Lisa Yin Zhang

Stories in the Seams: A People's History of Black Quilts and Their Makers by Sharbreon Plummer | Chronicle Books, 2026

In an opinion piece for Hyperallergic in June, Sharbreon Plummer argued that Black American quilts are inseparable from the inner lives of their makers. Organized into three parts, “memory,” “method,” and “medicine,” Stories in the Seams is the fruit of that pivotal reframing. This compassionate collection of essays, homages, and interviews with Black American quiltmakers centers their interiority as much as their technique. Plummer — who also participated in a roundtable in Routed West , featured in this list as well — traces these quilts’ influence on artists and writers like Romare Bearden and bell hooks. As she writes in her introduction, “Black quilts remind us that healing, connection, and creativity are still possible.” — Lakshmi Rivera Amin

article_text:
Advocacy-focused Watermelon Pictures is temporarily waiving its theatrical film rental fees and box office revenue share for the documentary “ American Doctor ,” giving venues the option to offer discounted or free tickets.

The campaign will span roughly 50 cities and run through the week of the United States’ midterm elections, from October 30 to November 5. Watermelon hopes to expand the film’s reach to spotlight the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, which “American Doctor” documents through the perspectives of three physicians traveling to the region to provide medical aid.

In addition to discounted theatrical admissions, Watermelon is also making “American Doctor” available to stream free for one week on its subscription-based streaming platform, Watermelon+. The digital release runs from October 30 to November 6. A video on-demand release will follow on November 10.

“By waiving theatrical fees and offering ‘American Doctor’ free on Watermelon+, we’re making it easier for exhibitors and audiences to access this important film during election week,” said Justin DiPietro, Watermelon’s executive VP. “At a time when the humanitarian issues it explores deserve greater attention, we want to encourage meaningful conversations and ensure this story reaches as many people as possible.”

Directed by Poh Si Teng, “American Doctor” follows three U.S.-based physicians — one Palestinian, one Jewish, and one Zoroastrian — who volunteer in Gaza to provide emergency medical care as Israel’s military attacks cripple the region’s medical infrastructure. The film earned positive reviews after its Sundance Film Festival premiere in January. IndieWire’s chief film critic David Ehrlich named “American Doctor” a Critics’ Pick in August , calling it “a bracing and essential documentary about treating the despair of an ongoing genocide.” The film has earned more than $500,000 at the domestic box office.

Watermelon previously offered complimentary screenings of “American Doctor” to healthcare workers and donated net theatrical proceeds from an entire weekend to the Palestinian American Medical Association. Founded in 2024, the distribution and production banner has handled several titles focusing on Gaza, including “From Ground Zero,” “Palestine 36” and “The Voice of Hind Rajab.”

article_text:
Marian Goodman Gallery has hired Ebony L. Haynes to be its first-ever senior director, global head of curatorial affairs. She will start at the gallery in late November.

Haynes is best known for running 52 Walker, a Kunsthalle-style exhibition space that was under the David Zwirner umbrella and had full curatorial autonomy as well as an all-Black staff. Opened in 2021, the Tribeca space mounted 17 exhibitions during its run, including solos for Kandis Williams, Nikita Gale, Bob Thompson, Arthur Jafa, Sara Cwynar, and Nicole Eisenman. Haynes’s 52 Walker exhibitions were often critically lauded.

The Eisenman exhibition was the last under the 52 Walker moniker. Earlier this year, ARTnews reported that the gallery had transitioned to being just another David Zwirner space after Haynes’s promotion to global head of curatorial projects the previous fall. The first show staged there was a solo for Isa Genzken, which opened in March.

“How do I say this? It’s Marian Goodman,” Haynes said when asked about her decision to join the gallery. “For a long time, it’s been a gallery that I’ve been truly inspired by [in terms of] the kinds of exhibitions they’ve done over the decades, and a lot of their artists have inspired my own practice.”

When she was devising the blueprint of 52 Walker, down to its letterhead, Haynes took inspiration from Schema (March 1966) , a series of conceptual poems by Dan Graham, who has shown with Marian Goodman since the late 1980s. “ Schema influenced a lot of my decision-making in how I wanted to frame materials,” she said, adding that the numbers running down the letterhead were meant to help visitors “think about the ways the space is helping you process information.”

At Marian Goodman, Haynes’s newly created role will see her work on “exhibitions and special initiatives that deepen and expand its international program,” per a release. Haynes described it more simply: “I hope to support the direction of the gallery in this new moment. I don’t think this gallery needs a huge paradigm shift. It’s just so elegant and steeped in canonical history.”

In addition to Haynes’s hiring, Marian Goodman Gallery announced that Rose Lord and Junette Tang will now be co-presidents, sharing responsibility for its strategic direction and leading its management team, which includes Haynes. Emily-Jane Kirwan, managing partner and head of sales, will leave the gallery to focus on cultural philanthropy.

“As we approach the Gallery’s 50th anniversary, we are excited to lead it together—building on what has made the Gallery distinctive while creating new opportunities for our artists and program,” Lord said in a statement. “We are extremely grateful to Emily-Jane for her vision throughout her 15-year tenure and the central role she has played in expanding sales and institutional and patron relationships. She has championed our artists through significant projects, and was instrumental in the establishment of our Tribeca flagship.”

The leadership change is the first major one since the death of founder Marian Goodman earlier this year. In 2021, Goodman took on the role of chief executive and announced a five-person partnership to lead the gallery. Philip Kaiser, a longtime museum curator who joined the enterprise in 2019, served as president until 2025, exiting as a result of that year’s LA wildfires. Leslie Nolen continues on as a partner and member of the management team.

“Ebony is a natural fit for the Gallery,” Tang said in a statement. “She brings a strong curatorial vision, intellectual rigor, and deep engagement with artists, which aligns with our approach. Her appointment also reflects where we want to go next: expanding the ways we support our artists, creating new contexts for their work, and bringing a new perspective to our program as we enter the Gallery’s next 50 years.”

Since Marian Goodman’s move to Tribeca in 2024, Haynes said she has gotten to know the team from visiting each other’s galleries, which are around the corner from each other. Now, as part of the team, she said she is looking forward to listening to what the gallery’s artists are excited about and programming the Tribeca space.

“Having the space to be a vessel or the catalyst to translate an artist’s intentions as best as possible is hard to do well, but it’s the most rewarding kind of exhibition to do,” she said. “I was privileged to do so many at 52 Walker and within David Zwirner globally. I’m looking forward to doing that with the Marian Goodman artists.”

She added, “It’s a very unique experience to have people like Rose and Junette, who worked with Marian for so long, bring me along to continue stewarding her vision with them. It just feels really special—I’m not taking that opportunity lightly.”

article_text:
If you were on the internet in 2015, you likely followed the twisty tale of the Wu-Tang Clan ‘s Once Upon a Time in Shaolin . The Staten Island hip-hop titans conceived of the album as a conceptual artwork, a protest against the cheapening of music in the age of widespread piracy. Rather than release the music to the general public, the work was sold at auction for a reported $2 million to a then-anonymous American buyer, seemingly proving that music could sell at the level of Picasso and Warhol.

It proved a Pyrrhic victory when the buyer was revealed to be the hated “pharma bro” Martin Shkreli. The episode was a bitter lesson for the group, resulting in resentment and division. Even Clan member Method Man said, “Fuck that album. … When music can’t be music and y’all turning it into something else, fuck that. Give it to the people, if they want to hear the shit, let them have it. Give it away free.” (He somewhat softened his stance recently, on finally hearing the album.)

A new Netflix documentary, The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable (2026), presents a long and shaggy ride through the experience. Directed by producer Joanna Natasegara and featuring RZA as an executive producer, the film proves a frustrating watch: no one involved seems to, even now, have thought much about the lessons from their attempt to hijack the art market, a sometimes unpredictable world they blundered into, seeming to know little about it while somehow assuming that’s where the big money was. “Contemporary art is worth millions by virtue of its exclusivity,” said the band at the time. Of course, a vanishingly small percentage of artworks of any era are priced at that level, but maybe their misconception is understandable, since the members’ art world reference points, at least judging by the way they are quoted in the film, seem to be restricted to Leonardo da Vinci, Picasso, and Warhol.

Many of the art world’s denizens could have warned them away from the stunt. Funnily enough, in 2017, during the whole dustup, Richard Prince disavowed an artwork he had sold to Ivanka Trump before her father’s entry into politics. Of course, by then it was too late to warn RZA.

The album’s sale is mentioned in the opening sequence, with audio of an unidentified interviewer calling it “one of the coolest stories in art history.” RZA explains the thinking: “We’ll make one single copy of the album, treat it like it’s the Mona Lisa . It was a combination of ideas that led to it. Me and my student Cilvaringz—won’t take all the credit.”

“Would you ever do it again?” asks the interviewer.

Says the rapper, in a loaded two-letter word, “Um …”

The Shaggy Tale of an Unfolding Mess

The film then doesn’t mention the album again for a full 55 minutes, instead plunging the viewer at great length into the life story of Dutch-Moroccan rapper-producer Tarik Azzougarh, one of the masterminds of the project, including his traumatic childhood experiences of racism and abuse.

The director found him compelling, she explains in press materials: “Over a long lunch in beautiful Marrakech, where he lived, Tarik told me the twists and turns of the album’s 30-year story, and I was fascinated. It wasn’t only a great story; it resonated with me personally as someone who grew up in the ’90s with mixed heritage. The Wu-Tang Clan often talk about being teenagers inspired by East Asian culture through movies, while Tarik and his friends had, in turn, been inspired by the Clan.”

Unfortunately, for my money, Azzougarh doesn’t ultimately prove a compelling presence on screen. “I figured that a doc would show my side of the story,” Azzougarh tells the off-camera director early on, in a characteristically not-quite-electrifying observation.

The film slowly relates that the aspiring rapper and superfan ingratiated himself into the band’s circles, flying to New York multiple times as a teenager for the purpose. He earned the sobriquet Cilvaringz and membership in the Killa Beez, a network of musicians in the extended Wu-Tang family, releasing his own records on their imprint as well as producing some of the Clan’s albums.

Once Upon a Time was packaged in a custom handcrafted silver box and traveled with all the pomp and security of a seven-figure artwork, as the film shows. Only one copy will ever legally exist, in a protest against the loss of music’s aura in the age of its digital reproducibility, to paraphrase German philosopher Walter Benjamin. The band sold the record via online auctioneer Paddle8 in 2015, with the stipulation that the buyer could not release it commercially for 88 years, though they could play it at listening parties.

In keeping with the fine art theme, the band staged a listening event at MoMA PS1, after which Complex described the record as “rich, layered, and sonically bombastic,” with a “rugged, hard-hitting sound” reminiscent of early Wu-Tang Clan albums. Writing for ARTnews , a slightly more skeptical Dan Duray noted, “There were plenty of unexpected samples, melodramatic horns, cheesy bits of kung-fu dialogue.” Snippets are audible in the documentary.

Then Shkreli was arrested, and some of the film’s funnier moments come with the discussion of Wu-Tang’s attempts to find a way to reverse the sale and get the music to the people, including a rumored clause in the contract by which either Clan members or actor Bill Murray could legally steal the record back.

In 2018, Shkreli was convicted of securities fraud and conspiracy, and the Department of Justice sold the record to help pay his reparations. In 2021, it sold, for some $4 million, to digital art and crypto collective PleasrDAO, in whose hands it remains today. The group’s late founder , Jamis Johnson, said in 2021 that “there’s not a world in which we don’t own this album.” The group has organized several listening events, at venues from the Museum of Old and New Art in Tasmania to the Angel Orensanz Center, housed in a 175-year-old former synagogue in New York.

So now Once Upon a Time in Shaolin , with all its contradictions and challenges, is PleasrDAO’s problem. In a video interview with ARTnews , the collective’s “chief pleasing officer,” Jamis’s brother Adrian Johnson, outlined the tricky position in which the group finds itself.

“We don’t want the record to be streamed,” he said. “The moment it is, it becomes another album.”

He went on, “Everything about it is a paradox: it’s for the people, but it’s also highly guarded. It’s quite a difficult job as stewards of this art to say, ‘How can we bring it to the people but not devalue it?,’ and I don’t believe that keeping it locked away is right. I also don’t believe making it freely available is right. So we are constantly looking for creative ways to share this with the people.”

For future activations, keep an eye on a dedicated website , and tune in to Netflix for the documentary, but don’t hold out for too much excitement. I give it a passing grade.

article_text:
Artículos

Primer vistazo a Ben Kingsley como El Mandarín en Iron Man 3

Julio Vélez

¿Se han imaginado cómo lucirá Ben Kingsley en el papel de El Mandarín en Iron Man 3? Se ha filtrado en la red la primera imagen del siniestro personaje.

Entertainment Weekley reveló la primera imagen del actor inglés Ben Kingsley interpretando a El Mandarín , malévolo personaje que finalmente enfrentará al Hombre de Hierro en la pantalla grande, en Iron Man 3 .

¿Qué les parece? Todo parece indicar que Marvel aplicó las palabras de Kevin Feige sobre no estereotipar al Mandarín como un personaje de ascendencia china, sino “como el simbolismo de varias culturas”.

Seguramente veremos mucho más de aquel monólogo de El Mandarín visto en Comic-Con , en el trailer de Iron Man 3 , pelicula escrita y dirigida por Shane Black. Lo mejor de esta nueva entrega es que elenco está integrado por Robert Downey Jr. , Gwyneth Paltrow, Don Cheadle, Jon Favreau, Ben Kingsley, Guy Pearce, James Badge Dale y Ashley Hamilton.

Julio Vélez Colaborador en web y revista Cine PREMIERE desde 2006. Me especializo en anime/manga, comics, doblaje, tecnología y videojuegos. Mis sagas favoritas: Doctor Who, Star Trek, Dragon Ball y Star Wars. Batimaníaco, geek ochentero y hardcore gamer.

article_text:
Born in 1954 in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, Cindy Sherman has built one of the most influential bodies of work in contemporary art by photographing herself without ever making self-portraits. A student at Buffalo State College, she turned from painting to photography, and in 1977, newly settled in New York, she began the “Untitled Film Stills,” 70 black-and-white images in which she posed as anonymous heroines of imaginary films. The series made her a central figure of the Pictures Generation. Working alone in her studio as model, makeup artist, costume designer and photographer, she has since used wigs, prosthetics and, later, digital tools to dissect the stereotypes of gender, age and class circulated by cinema, advertising and art history. Her work has been the subject of major retrospectives, including at the Museum of Modern Art in 2012 and at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris in 2020.

This segment comes from “Transformation,” an episode of the fifth season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in October 2009. It surveys some thirty years of Sherman’s untitled works, grouped into informally named series such as fairy tales, centerfolds, history portraits, Hollywood/Hampton types and clowns.

20 minutes, in English.

Video © Art21. More information on Cindy Sherman here.

article_text:
H ere is an entertaining, if very exhausting fantasy-caper about the fashion biz from Boots Riley, a madcap mile-a-minute melee of unadulterated ker-aziness. You might need a couple of ibuprofen and a lie-down afterwards. Demi Moore perhaps thought she was here getting a gamey starring role, comparable to her Oscar-nominated turn in the beauty-industry satire The Substance . In fact, the way the film is structured and edited, Moore is hardly more than a returning cameo, though a potent one.

She plays Christie Smith, a billionaire couture designer who has an office in a trendily designed city block which leans over at an experimental angle. Christie is the object of obsessive attention from “boosters”: supercool young outlaw women who, nettled by her arrogance, shoplift her clothes from upscale stores and sell them on at knockdown Robin Hood prices. They are Corvette (Keke Palmer), Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige), the latter having the superpower of, by holding her breath, turning herself into a white woman who is less likely to be challenged in a store; an interesting metaphor for what Frantz Fanon might have called black skin, white masks.

For all their savvy, the boosters have a soft spot for certain men in their lives, notably a charismatic community leader called Dr Jack (Don Cheadle), who is running a friendship self-help scheme that is actually a fraudulent pyramid scam. And Corvette is entranced by a laidback charmer and oral sex enthusiast played by LaKeith Stansfield, who turns out to be a demonic male succubus.

The boosters’ chaotic way of life becomes even more problematic when they realise they are up against what appears to be a rival thief from China; this is Jianhu (Poppy Liu), who wields a magic portal ring the size of a toilet seat which sucks all the clothes out of a store and teleports them back to China, where underpaid workers have been making them under scandalously bad conditions. Jianhu is protesting against Christie Smith’s exploitative employment practices – and by being forced to make common cause with her, the boosters find themselves in unexpected territory: the moral high ground.

This is a cacophonous, chaotic film which delivers a sensory overload of almost incoherently frantic onscreen activity, and it can be hard to take, though it is often funny. There’s enough material here for a 12-episode streaming show, and that may be where Riley may wish to take it – although it’s quite an experience at feature-film length, a compressed spectacle of hellzapoppin’ uproar.

editorial_title_zh: 2026年圣丹斯电影节：文化与产业
editorial_excerpt_zh: 肖像画廊：诸如《哈莱姆往事》、《我想要你的性》和《如果我离去他们会怀念我吗》等电影节亮点，为独立艺术提供了一剂慰藉。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "圣丹斯电影节长期以来一直充满矛盾。正如艾比·孙（Abby Sun）去年为《电影评论》（Film Comment）所写的那样，从20世纪70年代末作为犹他/美国电影节（Utah/U.S. Film Festival）发端以来，该活动的行为准则一直是一种特洛伊木马式的策略：“利用明星嘉宾来提升新的独立声音。”这始终是一个微妙的权宜之计，但在我参加过的八届电影节中（包括2021年和2022年的两次线上举办），人们越来越难以分清明星的光芒究竟是在照亮那些等待被发掘的电影，还是掩盖了它们的光彩。多年来，我设法在帕克城的展映片单中搜寻到了一些真正的瑰宝——加勒特·布拉德利（Garrett Bradley）的《美国》（America）、萨凡纳·莉夫（Savanah Leaf）的《大地母亲》（Earth Mama）、雷文·杰克逊（Raven Jackson）的《泥路皆盐味》（All Dirt Roads Taste of Salt）、亚伦·希姆伯格（Aaron Schimberg）的《异托邦》（A Different Man）以及里奇·佩皮亚特（Rich Peppiatt）的《凯纳卡普》（Kneecap）皆属此列——但今年，为了找到那些由新锐电影人创作的规模更小、更大胆的电影，人们不得不费力涉足的耀眼片单实在让人感到格外畏惧。圣丹斯官方环保袋将Disney+的标志直接印在“自豪流媒体播放独立电影”（Proudly Streaming Independent Cinema）这句话的下方，这种讽刺意味可谓恰到好处、辛辣十足。", "links": [{"text": "wrote", "url": "https://us.list-manage.com/xth4HLYTnyN?e=270138fa20&c2id=301fe5b7d78b1a07eec9479cf031d5a1"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "电影节的后勤状况也毫无帮助。尽管近年来圣丹斯的观众规模有所扩大，但其场地选择却在缩减。为了观看约翰·威尔逊（John Wilson）那部（非常优秀的）《混凝土的历史》（The History of Concrete）的媒体及产业场放映，我提前了近100分钟排队——这段时间我本可以轻松看完像沃尔特·汤普森-埃尔南德斯（Walter Thompson-Hernández）的《如果我离去他们会怀念我吗》（If I Go Will They Miss Me）这样的电影。值得庆幸的是，在一位朋友热情推荐后，我通过链接总算看成了汤普森-埃尔南德斯这部温柔、深思熟虑的第二部长片。排队浪费的时间，或是被困在主街（Main Street）那座宛如企业休息室幻境附近的交通堵塞中的大巴上，再加上参加电影节的高昂费用（在一周的住宿中，除非你像我在2019年那样和朋友挤在一张双层床的下铺，否则费用很容易超过2000美元），这些都加剧了1月帕克城严寒带来的不适感。这使得展映片单中通常充斥的那些公式化古怪电影——其中许多经过工作坊打磨而变得平庸，且早已打上了制片厂的烙印——让人感觉像是对士气的打击。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所有这些也就是说，如果明年搬迁至科罗拉多州博尔德能理顺参加电影节的这些诸多方面，我双手双脚赞成。但当然，圣丹斯本身只是问题的一部分——电影行业本身以企业合并和公共艺术资助的掏空为标志，正日益成为一个对不受底线约束的独立艺术极不友好的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "恰如其分的是，今年片单中最具话题度的一些作品，以自我反思的方式探讨了所谓文化产业的种种困顿——而且其中一些确实相当不错。在格雷格·阿拉基（Gregg Araki）在圣丹斯的第11次（！）入选作品《我想要你的性》（I Want Your Sex）中，一个足智多谋的虐恋艺术家埃里卡·特雷西（Erika Tracy，由奥利维亚·王尔德饰演，散发着邪恶气息）与她年轻、懦弱的画廊助理埃利奥特（由拥有一张完美小狗脸的库珀·霍夫曼饰演）之间那段“完全搞砸了”（Totally Fucked-Up）的关系，成了一个探索欲望不可同化的复杂性以及艺术界金钱伪饰的契机。对于一部阿拉基的电影来说，其中的BDSM（绑缚与调教、统治与臣服、施虐与受虐）场景某种程度上算得上温和——这里真正的诱惑在于权力博弈，而非肉体冒险。正如埃利奥特在某处对两名警察所说的那样，他在埃里卡手下遭受的操纵和羞辱是真实的，但也“挺带劲的”。（与此同时，画廊的另一位助理听到他没有信托基金时大惊失色：“你是一个……孤儿吗？”）在所有机智的双关语、疯狂的恶作剧和坎普风表演之中，这里蕴含着某种能够穿透关于电影中性爱话语的道德焦虑的东西：这是一种深刻的反思，反思了一个过于保守的社会如何剥夺我们的自我认知，而一个厚颜无耻的资本主义社会又如何剥夺我们的自尊。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于凯茜·闫（Cathy Yan）的《画廊主》（The Gallerist）却不能这么说，这是一部笨拙且自鸣得意的闹剧，讲述了一具尸体出人意料地在巴塞尔艺术展（Art Basel）上变成抢手货的故事。但其中有一个场景，两个富人在竞标战中将这件作品的价格推高到了荒谬绝伦的高度，这在电影节上却让人感到分外切身。当你看到制片厂斥资1200万美元买下一部电影时，比如奥利维亚·王尔德的《邀请函》（The Invite），你确实会纳闷还剩下什么可分。部分而言，这正是约翰·威尔逊在他的银幕长片首作中切入的角度。正如他在开场几分钟里所讲述的那样，这个噱头在于，为了延续他的HBO剧集《约翰·威尔逊的十万个怎么做》（How To with John Wilson）的成功，他着手制作——并为之寻找资金支持——一部关于某种物质的电影，这种物质如此无处不在且必不可少，以至于几乎隐形：混凝土。威尔逊在这部作品中的方法与那档电视节目相比有点过于熟悉——将讽刺性的视觉与言语观察串联成一场联想丰富、往往欢快非常的旅程——但《混凝土的历史》依然是一部纯粹的乐事。威尔逊真挚、不知疲倦的好奇心，以及他那种顺着一条线索无论通往何处都一追到底的“好，还有”（“yes, and”）倾向，令人精神振奋。只需比我们其他人更仔细地审视我们周围的地方和人，他就发现了无尽的奇特之处、新鲜事物和故事：一位混凝土公司的员工兼怀揣演员梦的人，我们跟随他进入了一个短片片场；一个从人行道上清除口香糖并顺便出售特色“口香糖清除者”（Gum Buster）葡萄酒的家伙；一个为撰写贺岁浪漫喜剧而设立的美国编剧工会（Writers Guild of America）工作坊，其陈腐的见解成了反复出现的笑料。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在威爾森尋找金子時的某個節點，他收到了一項附帶條件的提案：必須加入一條關於某位知名音樂人的故事線，因為當前以音樂明星為主角的名人傳記片正大行其道。查莉·XCX（Charli xcx）在她那部以音樂與電影界為背景的諷刺片《The Moment》中也處理了類似的要求。該片由艾丹·扎米里（Aidan Zamiri）執導、這位流行巨星擔任製片人，講述了查莉在她的 2024 年專輯《brat》取得姍姍來遲且勢不可擋的巨大成功之後，如何像威爾森那樣努力維持其熱度。正當她為自己有史以來規模最大的世界巡演做準備時，她的唱片公司與亞馬遜米高梅工作室（Amazon MGM Studios）達成了一項紀錄片交易，並聘請了一位擅長拍攝平淡無奇、廣泛傳播的演唱會電影的導演（由亞歷山大·斯卡斯加德飾演）。大眾吸引力的誘惑與這位 365 派對女孩（365 party girl）張揚且挑釁的品牌形象在一部機智敏捷、隨著查莉的俱樂部音樂節奏律動的電影中發生了碰撞。正當你以為這部電影要滑向可憐的小富婆式感傷時，它卻來了一個轉折，其黑色喜劇式的憤世嫉俗令人耳目一新——尤其是在當前這個充斥著流行天后們自導自演或以她們為主角、歌頌她們女老闆（girlboss）成就的紀錄片的串流媒體環境中（對照組：珍妮佛·洛佩茲、碧昂絲、泰勒絲……）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "已故導演威廉·格里夫斯（William Greaves）早在 1995 年就曾指出：「不幸的是，世界似乎正日益以利潤為導向，這對電影造成的影響是毀滅性的。它確實對我的真相造成了嚴重破壞。」然而，格里夫斯卻是少數能夠在無情變幻的行業中設法保留其真相的作者導演之一，他受託參與了無數電視紀錄片和教育影片的創作（其中許多作品，例如公共事務新聞節目《Black Journal》，本身就被證明具有開創性），藉此來支撐他自己的熱情項目，其中包括無與倫比的《Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One》（1968）。然而，他的其中一個此類項目卻因資金問題生前未見天日。1972 年，格里夫斯邀請了哈萊姆文藝復興時期的許多在世名流——演員雷伊·惠珀（Leigh Whipper）、社會主義領袖理查·B·摩爾（Richard B. Moore）、詩人阿爾納·邦蒂姆斯（Arna Bontemps）、攝影師傑克·范德澤（Jack Van der Zee）等人——來到杜克·艾靈頓（Duke Ellington）家中舉辦派對。當身穿盛裝的嘉賓們交際應酬、追憶非洲裔美國人文化繁榮那段非凡且來之不易的時期時，格里夫斯與他的兒子大衛以及其他三位攝影師將其拍攝了下來。這些素材一直躺在格里夫斯的檔案館中，直到大衛和他的女兒莉亞尼·格里夫斯（Liani Greaves）將其修復並重新剪輯成一部光彩奪目的真實主義紀錄片：《哈萊姆往事》（Once Upon a Time in Harlem），該片在本屆日舞影展上首映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "這部傑出的電影中有許多令人讚嘆之處：它以自己的方式具有自我反思性，卻沒有一絲諷刺的瑕疵；色彩豐富；鏡頭遊移而親密；派對場景與對各界嘉賓的談話頭採訪進行了細緻的穿插剪輯；詩歌的運用增添了超越時間的維度；討論本身則在不敬與嚴謹之間、在酒後狂歡與嚴肅的政治辯論之間自如切換。觀看《哈萊姆往事》所帶來的壓倒性感受就像是收到了一份禮物——這是一種罕見的、雙重回溯式的目光，透過 1970 年代的時代精神回望 1920 年代的時代精神。這彷彿是將那些見證過、深知太多的長者之靈召喚回來，以便與我們分享他們的智慧。這讓人不禁思考：有多少這樣的人物、多少這樣的故事正在檔案館中積滿灰塵，或者更糟的是，迷失在時間的風中？《哈萊姆》提醒我們，電影遠不止是一種商品或娛樂來源。它是一種永存的防腐處理，也是致後世的一封信函。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在本屆日舞影展的眾多發現中，有兩部低調的作品脫穎而出，兩者皆為父子故事。《封閉》（Closure）是波蘭導演米哈烏·馬爾恰克（Michał Marczak）的最新非虛構長片，以非凡的親密感與優雅，追蹤了一位父親對一年多前失蹤的十幾歲兒子的不懈尋找。正當犯罪敘事——這是繼名人肖像之後的另一當前紀錄片產業風潮——聚焦於誰、在哪裡以及為什麼時，《封閉》處理的則是在沒有清晰解釋的情況下生活、並去面對其他人（甚至是我們所愛的人）之不可知性意味著什麼。於聚焦創新獨立電影的 NEXT 單元首映的《如果我走了他們會想念我嗎》（If I Go Will They Miss Me）同樣是一部迴避簡單答案的電影。故事設定在洛杉磯的沃茨（Watts）社區，追蹤了小安特（Lil Ant）——一個喜愛白日夢與繪畫的男孩——與他的父親大安特（Big Ant）之間緊張的關係；後者剛結束漫長的牢獄生涯歸來，正掙扎著適應父親和丈夫的角色。這部電影是一曲關於男子氣概的安靜而揪心的沉思，同時堅持了兩個真理：個人對自己的行為擁有能動性與責任，但他們同時也是環境的產物。它挑戰我們去尋找那種監獄工業複合體所不允許的同理心——一種不以人們的過去為條件、而是對他們的未來抱持堅韌希望的同理心。如果《哈萊姆往事》、《封閉》以及《如果我走了他們會想念我嗎》能夠找到應得的觀眾，那麼這個行業或許終究還有值得支持的地方。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
The Sundance Film Festival has long been full of contradictions. As Abby Sun wrote for Film Comment last year, from its origins as the Utah/U.S. Film Festival in the late 1970s, the event’s M.O. has been a kind of Trojan horse: “use star guests to elevate new independent voices.” That has always been a delicate ploy, but in the eight editions that I’ve attended (including two virtual editions in 2021 and 2022), it’s been increasingly hard to tell if the star power is illuminating or outshining the films poised for discovery. Over the years, I’ve managed to forage some true gems in the Park City lineups—Garrett Bradley’s America , Savanah Leaf’s Earth Mama , Raven Jackson’s All Dirt Roads Taste of Salt , Aaron Schimberg’s A Different Man , and Rich Peppiatt’s Kneecap all come to mind—but this year, the number of glitzy titles one had to wade through to get to the smaller, bolder films by newer filmmakers felt especially daunting. The official Sundance tote’s placement of the Disney+ logo directly below the words “Proudly Streaming Independent Cinema” was appropriately pungent with irony.

The festival’s logistics don’t help. While the Sundance audience has grown in size in recent years, its venue options have shrunk. I lined up nearly 100 minutes in advance for the press-and-industry screening of John Wilson’s (very good) The History of Concrete —a window of time in which I could have easily watched a film like Walter Thompson-Hernández’s If I Go Will They Miss Me . Thankfully, I managed to catch Thompson-Hernández’s gentle, thoughtful sophomore feature on a link after a friend enthusiastically recommended it to me. Time lost in queues or on buses stuck in traffic near the corporate-lounge fantasia that is Main Street, along with exorbitant costs of attending the festival (easily upwards of two grand for a weeklong stay, unless you squeeze into the bottom bunk of a bunk bed with a friend, as I did in 2019), add to the discomfort of the freezing cold of Park City in January. This can make the lineup’s usual preponderance of formulaically quirky films, many of them workshopped into banality and already stamped with studio logos, feel like assaults to one’s morale.

All of which is to say that if next year’s relocation to Boulder, Colorado smooths out any of these aspects of attending the festival, I’m all for it. But of course, Sundance itself is only part of the problem—the film business itself, marked by the agglomeration of corporations and the gutting of public arts funding, is becoming an increasingly unfriendly place for independent art unconstrained by the bottom line.

Fittingly, some of the buzziest titles in this year’s lineup grappled, self-reflexively, with the travails of the so-called culture industry—and some were actually pretty good. In Gregg Araki’s 11th (!) selection at Sundance, I Want Your Sex , the Totally Fucked-Up relationship between a wily dominatrix-artist, Erika Tracy (Olivia Wilde, exuding maleficence), and her young, milquetoast gallery assistant, Elliot (a perfectly puppy-faced Cooper Hoffman), becomes an occasion to explore both the unassimilable complexities of desire and the moneyed pretenses of the art world. The BDSM scenes are somewhat tame for an Araki film—the real seduction here is in plays of power, rather than adventures of the flesh. Elliot’s manipulation and humiliation at the hands of Erika is real, but also kinda hot , as he says at one point to a pair of cops. (Meanwhile, a fellow assistant at the gallery is shocked to hear that he doesn’t have a trust fund: “Are you an… orphan?”) Amid all of the witty one-liners, wild hijinks, and campy performances, there is something here that cuts through the moral hand-wringing of the sex-in-cinema discourse: a profound reflection on the ways in which an overly prudish society denies us self-knowledge, while a brazenly capitalist society denies us self-respect.

The same cannot be said for Cathy Yan’s The Gallerist , a ham-fisted and smug caper about a corpse turned, improbably, into a hot item at Art Basel. But one scene, in which two wealthy men drive up the price of the piece to obscene heights in a bidding war, hit close to home at the festival. When you see studios shelling out $12 million to buy a single film, like Olivia Wilde’s The Invite , you do wonder what’s left to go around. That, partly, is what John Wilson gets at with his debut theatrical feature. The schtick, as he narrates it in the opening minutes, is that in an attempt to follow up on the success of his HBO series, How To with John Wilson , he set out to make—and find financiers for—a movie about a substance so omnipresent and essential as to be almost invisible: concrete. Wilson’s methods here are a little too familiar from the TV show—ironic visual and verbal observations strung together into an associative, often rollicking ride—but The History of Concrete is still an unadulterated pleasure. Wilson’s genuine, indefatigable curiosity, as well as his “yes, and” tendency to follow a thread wherever it leads, is invigorating. Just by looking a little harder than the rest of us at the places and people around us, he finds endless eccentricities, novelties, and stories: a worker at a concrete company and aspiring actor, whom we follow onto a short-film set; a guy who removes chewing gum from sidewalks and also sells speciality “Gum Buster” wine; a Writers Guild of America workshop for writing Hallmark rom-coms whose hackneyed insights become recurring gags.

At one point in Wilson’s on-screen quests to find a funder, he receives an offer conditional upon the inclusion of a storyline about a musician of considerable renown, given that celebrity biopics about music stars are currently all the rage. Charli xcx deals with similar demands in her music-and-film-world satire The Moment . Directed by Aidan Zamiri and produced by the pop star, the film finds Charli contending, Wilson-like, with staying relevant after the long-overdue and overwhelming success of her 2024 album brat . While she prepares for her biggest world tour ever, her label strikes a deal with Amazon MGM Studios for a documentary, and hires a director (played by Alexander Skarsgård) of anodyne, widely streamed concert films. The allure of mass appeal clashes with the 365 party girl’s brash and provocative brand in a quick-witted film that moves and pulsates to the rhythm of Charli’s club music. Just when you think the movie is slipping into poor-little-rich-girl sentimentality, it takes a swerve that is refreshing in its black-comedic cynicism—particularly in a streaming landscape crowded with docs by and about pop divas that aggrandize their girlboss achievements (cf: Jennifer Lopez, Beyoncé, Taylor Swift…).

The late director William Greaves said as far back as 1995 that, “unhappily, the world seems progressively oriented to the bottom line, and the impact on cinema is devastating. It sure plays havoc with my truth.” Yet Greaves was one of those rare auteurs who found ways to preserve his truth even in a ruthlessly changing industry, working on innumerable TV documentaries and educational films on commission (many of which, like the public-affairs news show Black Journal , proved pioneering in their own right) so he could make his passion projects, including the utterly singular Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One (1968). One such project of his, however, never saw the light of day during his lifetime due to funding issues. In 1972, Greaves invited many of the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance—actor Leigh Whipper, socialist leader Richard B. Moore, poet Arna Bontemps, photographer Jack Van der Zee, and others—to Duke Ellington’s home for a party. As the guests, dressed to the nines, hobnobbed and reminisced about that extraordinary and hard-won period of African-American cultural flourishing, Greaves, along with his son David and three other cameramen, filmed them. That footage lay in Greaves’s archives until David and his daughter Liani Greaves restored and restitched it together into a resplendent verité documentary: Once Upon a Time in Harlem , which premiered at this year’s Sundance.

There is much to admire in this brilliant movie, self-reflexive in its own way but without the taint of irony: rich colors; roving and intimate camerawork; the careful sequencing of party scenes interspersed with talking-head interviews with various guests; the use of poetry, which adds a timeless dimension; and the discussions themselves, which oscillate with remarkable ease between irreverence and intellectual rigor, between drunken revelry and serious political debate. The overwhelming effect of watching Once Upon a Time in Harlem is that of receiving a gift—a rare, doubly retrospective look back at the zeitgeist of the 1920s through that of the 1970s. It’s as if the ghosts of elders, who saw and knew so much, have been summoned so they can share their wisdom with us. It makes you wonder: how many such figures, how many such stories, are gathering dust in vaults, or worse, lost to the winds of time? Harlem is a reminder that cinema is much more than a commodity or a source of entertainment. It is a kind of embalmment, and a missive to posterity.

Among the discoveries at this year’s Sundance, two under-the-radar titles, both father-son tales, stood out to me. Closure , the latest nonfiction feature by Polish director Michał Marczak, follows a father’s relentless search for a teenage son who went missing over a year before with remarkable intimacy and elegance. Where true-crime narratives—the other current doc-industry fad, alongside celeb portraits—fixate on the who, where, and why of it all, Closure deals with what it means to live without neat explanations and confront the unknowability of other people, even those we love. If I Go Will They Miss Me , which premiered in the NEXT section for innovative indies, is also a film that evades simple answers. Set in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, it traces the fraught relationship between Lil Ant, a boy who loves to daydream and draw, and his dad Big Ant, who has just returned from a long stint in prison and struggles to inhabit the roles of father and husband. The film is a quiet, wrenching meditation on masculinity that holds two truths at once: individuals have agency and responsibility over their actions, and they are also products of their circumstances. It challenges us to find the kind of empathy that the prison-industrial complex disallows—one that isn’t conditional upon people’s pasts, but rather, is resilient in its hope for their futures. If Once Upon a Time in Harlem , Closure , and If I Go Will They Miss Me find the audiences they deserve, then there still might be something worth rooting for in this biz after all.

article_text:
Nato nel 1983 a Lahore in Pakistan, a vent’anni Salman Toor si trasferisce negli Stati Uniti. Inizialmente la trasferta era finalizzata ad approfondire la sua conoscenza dell’arte occidentale, poi l’America è divenuto il luogo eletto a residenza permanente, anche perché più sicuro per vivere dopo il suo coming out, avvenuto con l’ausilio di colori e pennelli.

Il salto è lungo sia geograficamente sia culturalmente. Tuttavia, tradizioni così diverse da entrare spesso in conflitto si riconciliano sulle sue tele in immagini che sono difficili da osservare nel mondo reale ma emergono dal mescolarsi di ricordi e desideri.

Fra i pittori contemporanei della sua generazione, Toor spicca per la sua capacità di generare uno stile definito e riconoscibile attraverso l’utilizzo estremamente personale, spesso intimo, di storie e palette . Va dato merito alla Courtauld Gallery di Londra per avere organizzato la sua prima mostra personale europea, Someone Like You , che durerà fino al 10 gennaio. Diciannove quadri, integrati da disegni e bozzetti in un’altra sala della Courtauld, presentano questo artista con opere che spaziano dal 2019 al 2026.

Una delle multiple abilità di Toor consiste nell’inserire armoniosamente oggetti contemporanei come telefoni cellulari e computer in atmosfere che traggono ispirazione dal confronto con pittori di altre epoche. L’utilizzo della luce di un computer portatile per illuminare lateralmente il gioco di Pillow Fight ( Battaglia con i Cuscini , del 2022) è solo uno degli esempi ben riusciti di questa destrezza.

Nei quadri in mostra queste apparecchiature sostituiscono fonti di luce che nel passato sarebbero state raffigurate come candele o lampadine: nel tondo Lunch , del 2019, quella che sembra un scena conviviale classica è in realtà il ritratto di tre amici intorno a un tavolo, in cui uno mostra agli altri qualcosa sul suo cellulare, da cui proviene il chiarore centrale dell’opera.

La tecnologia non viene utilizzata come un’eccentricità ma come parte integrante della nostra vita quotidiana e ausilio costante delle nostre interazioni sociali. Questo vale ancora di più nei contesti che sono raffigurati in questa esposizione.

Nella prima sala si fronteggiano due degli ambienti ricorrenti nelle sue opere: i desk aeroportuali per l’immigrazione e i bar gay di New York. Anche in questi casi, Toor offre una rappresentazione emotivamente efficace delle sensazioni e dei luoghi, fisici e mentali, attraversati dai personaggi ritratti.

Man with Face Creams and Phone Plug ( Uomo con Creme per il Viso e Cavo del Telefono ) mostra la situazione apparentemente priva di drammi ma oggettivamente umiliante, di un ragazzo proveniente dall’Asia meridionale che deve svuotare completamente le tasche al controllo di ingresso negli Stati Uniti. I suoi oggetti, dal caricatore del cellulare agli altri effetti personali fra i quali si evidenziano i prodotti cosmetici, narrano una storia ricca di dettagli da interpretare.

A riflettere e ampliare questa immagine, troviamo accanto Group B , un quadro popolato da più persone in attesa. Non scorgiamo rabbia ma un misto di tristezza e rassegnazione, più stanchezza che disagio. É ricorrente la presenza di personaggi chiaramente LGBT+, che come nel suo caso stanno cercando di trasferirsi in luoghi più sicuri di quelli natali.

Superati i controlli alla frontiera, ci spostiamo sul muro di fronte, con Bar Boy posto accanto a The Bar on the East 13th : scene di locali gay dove alcuni degli avventori hanno trovato compagnia mentre altri rimangono a guardare il cellulare nella speranza di uscire dalla solitudine. Il barista della seconda opera si può prontamente confrontare con la sua collega parigina di oltre un secolo prima che si trova nella sala adiacente della Courtauld, in Un bar aux Folies Bergère , dipinto da Édouard Manet nel 1882.

I riferimenti ad artisti che lo hanno preceduto sono talvolta ravvisabili nello stile e in altri casi espliciti: in Museum Boys pone al centro dell’attenzione una Fontana di Marcel Duchamp accanto a oggetti che ricordano opere di altri artisti, in una teca condivisa con i corpi di due uomini abbracciati.

Lahore e New York si incontrano sulla tela, contrastando col pennello l’impossibilità di vivere e amare liberamente nei luoghi di origine.

In The Women , tre giovani donne chiacchierano adagiate su un letto matrimoniale mentre un adolescente rimane in piedi davanti a una cassettiera e a uno specchio, esaminando dei cosmetici. Back Lawn ( Il Prato Dietro Casa ) mostra una placida sera a Lahore, in cui da una parte la famiglia cena all’aperto mentre due ragazzi si abbracciano amorevolmente sotto una tenda nascosta dalla vegetazione.

Sono tasselli di una storia che si dipana attraverso i continenti, fino a coincidere con la scena di Three Friends in a Cab ( Tre Amici in un Taxi ), in cui tre uomini attraversano uno dei ponti di New York per andare a passare una serata senza timori o proibizioni. Nel sedile posteriore del taxi, le tinte scure si diluiscono in sorrisi.

article_text:
写真家、映像作家、音楽家として活動する中野道の写真展「めいめつ」が、2026年10月9日から22日まで東京・代官山のSISON GALLERyで開催される。自身の時間のなかに現れては消えていった人や風景を見つめながら、「記録」と「記憶」のあいだをたどる展覧会だ。

アメリカ・ノースカロライナ州に生まれ、長野県松本市で育った中野。幼少期を過ごした松本の野山、写真との出会い、身近な人との別れなど、自身の経験や記憶を起点として写真や映像、音楽による表現を続けてきた。中野は「写真は、記録であり、記憶でもある」と語る。シャッターを切った瞬間、そこに存在していた時間は過去へと変わり、写真だけが残される。しかし写真を見返すことで、フレームには写っていない前後の時間や当時の感情までもが立ち上がり、記憶そのものが更新されていくという。

本展で中野がたどるのは、写真に残すことのできたものと、その周縁に存在する「残せなかったもの」だ。かつて共に過ごした人々、すでに戻ることのできない時間、見えているものと見えなくなったもの。それらを写真によって往還しながら、自身が過ごしてきた時間にひとつの区切りをつけようとする。

背景にあるのは、老いや喪失に対する意識の変化だ。自身の白髪、飼っていた犬の死、祖父の葬儀、年齢を重ねた祖母や母の姿。かつて永遠に続くと思っていた時間が失われていくなか、中野は「僕が集めていたのは、自分がもう戻れなくなる時間だった」と記す。展覧会タイトルの「めいめつ」は、消えていくものと、それでもまだ残っている光を見つめようとする眼差しを示している。

中野自身、本展について「自分の青春にさよならするようなもの」と位置づける。過去を保存するためだけではなく、失われていくことを受け入れながら、それでもなお光っている時間を写真にとどめる。その行為を通して、記憶、時間、喪失という中野が継続してきたテーマに向き合う。

中野は上智大学大学院文学研究科修士課程修了後、2015年から写真と映像を中心に制作活動を開始。2020年に写真集『あかつき』、2023年に『Days in Between』を刊行した。現在は東京とニューヨークを拠点に活動し、音楽ではバンドModern Jazz Warのフロントマンも務めている。

タイトル

中野道「めいめつ」

場所

SISON GALLERy（東京都渋谷区猿楽町3-18）

会期

2026年10月9日（金）〜22日（木）

時間

13:00〜18:00（最終日17:00まで）

休み

月・火曜日

料金

無料

URL

https://sison.tokyo/

Lin）被罢免了公司电影部门负责人职务。在Netflix上周进行6%的员工裁减（其受害者包括首席内容官贝拉·巴贾里亚和林的得力助手道格·贝尔格拉德）之后，各方共识认为联合首席执行官泰德·萨兰多斯让林卷铺走人只是时间问题。这只花了一天时间。据三位知情人士向《综艺》透露，在周四巴贾里亚离职的消息传出后，萨兰多斯于周五给林打电话，告知他已被解雇。这位高管昂首挺胸、在周末继续坚持工作，出席了周六的学院晚宴（与萨兰多斯身处同一房间）并出席了周日的业内意见领袖放映会，以支持《黑球》（“La Bola Negra”）的电影制片人。正如关于Netflix清洗行动的许多文章所总结的那样，在该平台股价表现不佳和用户参与度下降的背景下，公司的创意领导层正在经历全面改组。资深电影和电视高管彼得·赖斯现在将负责并整顿该平台的内容。关于林为何被解雇的各种说法甚嚣尘上，但它们得出了相同的结论：归根结底，这行不通。尽管林完成了他削减开支并制作能与订阅用户产生共鸣的电影的指令。在解雇林和巴贾里亚并迎来赖斯之后，一些人说萨兰多斯急于向华尔街兜售一个关于增长的故事（Netflix的季度财报将于周二发布）。另有人说，林舞得不够快，无法在黏性的流媒体作品和院线上映实验之间找到平衡（平心而论，他在一份为期五年的合同中只走了一半，按当今的标准来看，这勉强够把演员阵容公告凑齐）。围绕他与格蕾塔·韦格维（Greta Gerwig）和本·阿弗莱克等一线电影人据称存在的紧张关系，也有一些有趣的泄密，我们稍后会谈到。Netflix的林时代是以紧缩为特征的，无论是好莱坞的评价，还是从这位《乐高大电影》制片人自己的角度来看。《纽约时报》6月的一篇人物专访宣称，林不再“纵容”好莱坞，并夸耀他既不“对明星献殷勤，也不开空头支票”。其暗含的意思是，他的前任斯科特·斯图伯在2022年为人才支付了过高的报酬，并且过于雄心勃勃地承诺在2022年每周上映一部新的Netflix电影。这些努力逐渐缩减，直到斯图伯在2024年中期离职。相传，林带着红笔和砍刀上任，希望能强调重质不重量。有些人觉得凑巧的是，斯图伯的政治遗产至今仍被热议，或许是为了给林及其前老板巴贾里亚做出的决定提供掩护。在一片喧嚣的当前Netflix裁员声中，一位多话的片厂消息人士表示，重要的是要记住，很长很长一段时间里Netflix的主导逻辑是“我们根本不在乎院线”。在影院上映电影从来都不是Netflix商业模式的一部分。斯图伯支付了溢价，将马丁·斯科塞斯、阿方索·卡隆和雷恩·约翰逊等电影人吸引到该平台上。他还狂热地致力于让院线放映商以任何身份接受Netflix的作品。虽然他们当时拒绝了，但熟悉萨兰多斯的人士表示，斯图伯为不可避免的趋势奠定了基础——围绕电影创造价值的唯一途径，就是先将它们搬上银幕。了解林情况的人士称，林将这一逻辑付诸实现，说服萨兰多斯相信，家庭导向的IP在转向流媒体之前，应该获得强劲且独家的院线窗口期。我们将在明年看到成果，届时格韦格的《纳尼亚传奇：魔法师的外甥》（“Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew”）和《查理和巧克力工厂》将登陆各大影城。Netflix过去曾按项目的预算范围来组织其内部电影团队，而林则根据类型专长将高管分组。他还迅速安排了因斯图伯离职而空缺的发行窗口期（《Nonnas》、《欢乐乡村2》、《星期四谋杀俱乐部》）。他每周花一天时间与Netflix动画团队在一起，在那里他任命汉娜·明海拉为领导者。对于核心片单，林因争取到阿兰·里奇森（《战争机器》）、马修·麦康纳和本·斯蒂勒参与即将推出的项目而受到赞誉。在其离职前的几周里，有报道称林与电影人阿弗莱克（刚上映的《动物》的导演）因使用其AI平台InterPositive而发生冲突。或许更具冲击力的是，今年夏天他与格韦格围绕即将上映的《纳尼亚》产生了裂痕。这部电影代表了一场2.5亿美元的院线优先豪赌。四位知情人士表示，事实上，林和格韦格今年早些时候曾在一场关于该项目的Zoom通话中闹翻。据称，在一次有众多Netflix高管参加的虚拟会议上，林在讨论电影进展的对话中对这位导演表现得“轻蔑”。业内皆知林极其公正，但有时直言不讳显得有些愚钝。消息不胫而走消息很快在奈飞内部传开，称那次会议不欢而散，消息人士称，巴贾里亚随后致电格维格的制片人艾米·帕斯卡尔（Amy Pascal）以平息事态。还有两位消息人士透露，格维格的新任、权势熏天的CAA经纪人布莱恩·洛尔德（Bryan Lourd）因这一失误直接找了萨兰多斯。所有消息人士均一致表示，林随后便被排除在该片之外，贝尔格拉德则介入成为监督该项目的奈飞主要高管（当然，直到他上周被裁）。没有哪个消息人士暗示这一事件直接导致了林的被解雇。林的一位辩护者称，他从“不害怕讨论如何把电影拍得更好”。另一位熟悉该公司的人士则表示，有不少电影人对林的表达方式也有过类似的看法。虽然人们可能会津津乐道地猜测，格维格在颠覆之作《芭比》之后的下一部作品可能会遇到麻烦，但不要忘记，在上映周末到来之前，业界一直对那部由玛格特·罗比主演的电影持怀疑态度。《芭比》在全球斩获14.4亿美元票房，并成为华纳兄弟影片公司历史上票房最高的作品。虽然话题会瞬间转到林的接替者是谁（是迈克·德·卢卡和帕姆·阿布迪吗？“很可能是，”一位高层消息人士说），但也不必为林洒下太多同情之泪。他是从自己在Rideback取得成功的白手起家的事业中晋升到奈飞的。“当我接下这份工作时，贝拉给了我一条简单的建议：做你自己，”林在Variety获得的一份周一内部备忘录中写道。“你们在这里工作是因为它关乎个人。正是由于你们对电影的个人热爱与我们服务的观众之间那种心照不宣的契约。对他们而言，电影无关生意。它们关乎感受。”", article_text:
“Everyone is collateral damage.” That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the company’s head of film. Following last week’s 6% workforce reduction at Netflix – which claimed victims including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and Lin’s right-hand Doug Belgrad – consensus said it was a matter of time before co-CEO Ted Sarandos would show Lin the door. It took a day. On the heels of the Bajaria news on Thursday, Sarandos rang Lin on Friday to tell him he’d been dismissed, three sources told Variety . The exec kept his head up and pressed on through the weekend, appearing at Saturday’s Academy Gala (in the same room as Sarandos) and at a Sunday tastemaker screening to support the filmmakers of “La Bola Negra.” As has been summarized in many articles about the Netflix purge, creative leadership at the company is being overhauled amid poor stock performance and declining user engagement on the platform. Peter Rice, the veteran film and TV executive, will now preside over and shake up the platform’s content. Competing narratives are flying about why Lin was let go, but they arrive at the same conclusion: In the end, it wasn’t working. This, despite Lin meeting his mandates to curb spending and make movies that resonated with subscribers. In firing Lin and Bajaria and ushering in Rice, some say Sarandos was desperate to sell a story about growth to Wall Street (Netflix’s quarterly earnings report drops Tuesday). Others say Lin could not dance fast enough to find the balance between sticky streaming titles and theatrical release experiments (in fairness, he made it halfway through a five-year deal, barely enough time to get a casting announcement together by today’s standards). There are also some interesting leaks around tension he’s said to have with A-list filmmakers like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck, which we’ll get to. The Lin era at Netflix was framed around austerity, both by the town and in some ways by “The Lego Movie” producer himself. A June profile in the New York Times declared Lin was done “coddling” Hollywood, bragging he did not “fawn over stars or write blank checks.” The implication was that his predecessor Scott Stuber had overpaid for talent and too-ambitiously committed to a new Netflix movie release every week in 2022. Those efforts scaled back gradually until Stuber exited in mid-2024. Lin entered with a red pen and a machete, the lore goes, in hopes of emphasizing quality over quantity. Some find it convenient that Stuber’s legacy is still being kicked up, perhaps to provide cloud cover for decisions made by Lin and his former boss Bajaria. Amid the noise of the current Netflix layoffs, it’s important to remember that the prevailing logic at Netflix for a long, long time was “we don’t give a shit about theatrical,” said one colorful studio source. Releasing movies in theaters was never part of the Netflix business model. Stuber paid premiums to get filmmakers like Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón and Rian Johnson on the service. He also worked with fervor to make the theatrical exhibitors accept Netflix titles in any capacity. While they refused at the time, individuals familiar with Sarandos said Stuber laid the groundwork for the inevitable – that the only way to create value around movies is to put them in theaters first. Lin brought this logic to fruition in convincing Sarandos that family-driven IP should receive robust, exclusive theatrical windows before moving on to streaming, individuals with knowledge of Lin said. We’ll see the results next year when Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” come to cineplexes. Where Netflix once organized its internal film teams by the budget range of projects they worked on, Lin grouped his executives according to genre expertise. He also moved swiftly to program release windows left empty by Stuber’s exit (“Nonnas,” “Happy Gilmore 2,” “The Thursday Murder Club”). He spent one day of his work week with the Netflix animation team, where he installed Hannah Minghella as a leader. For the core slate, Lin is credited with wooing Alan Ritchson (“War Machine”), Matthew McConaughey and Ben Stiller for upcoming projects. In the weeks before his exit, reports said Lin clashed with filmmaker Affleck (director of the just-released “Animals”) over the use of his AI platform InterPositive. Perhaps more consequential was a rift with Gerwig this summer over the upcoming “Narnia.” The movie represents a $250 million theatrical-first gamble. Four sources with knowledge of the matter said that, indeed, Lin and Gerwig had a falling out during a Zoom call about the project earlier this year. On a virtual meeting populated by numerous Netflix executives, Lin is said to have been “dismissive” to the director in conversation about the progress of the film. Lin is known in town to be incredibly fair, but at times obtuse in his frankness. Word travelled fast around Netflix that the meeting had gone south, at which point sources said Bajaria called Gerwig’s producer Amy Pascal to smooth things over. Two sources also said that Gerwig’s new, all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd went to Sarandos directly over the faux pas. Lin was subsequently disappeared from the film, all sources concurred, and Belgrad stepped in as the primary Netflix exec overseeing the project (until, of course, he was laid off last week). None of the sources suggested the incident led to Lin’s firing. One Lin defender said he’s never “afraid to talk about how to make a movie better.” Another person familiar with the company said there are any number of filmmakers who could say the same about Lin’s delivery. While it may be juicy to speculate that Gerwig’s follow-up to the game changer “Barbie” could be troubled, don’t forget that the industry doubted that Margot Robbie film right up to opening weekend. “Barbie” grossed $1.44 billion at the worldwide box office and became the highest-earning release in the history of Warner Bros. Pictures. While talk will instantly turn to Lin’s replacement (is it Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy? “Probably,” said one high-placed source), don’t shed too many tears for Lin. He ascended to Netflix from a successful, self-made business in Rideback. “When I took this job, Bela gave me a simple piece of advice: Be yourself,” Lin wrote in a Monday memo obtained by Variety . “You work here because it’s personal. Because of that unspoken pact between your individual passion for movies and the audiences we serve. To them, movies aren’t about business. They’re about feeling something.”

article_text:
Paramount Pictures’ upcoming “ Call of Duty ” movie, based on the massively popular video game franchise, is definitely not going to feel like a comic book tentpole or make soldiers out to be superheroes, director Peter Berg recently told ComicBook . The “Friday Night Lights” and “Lone Survivor” director is helming the video game adaptation from a script by Taylor Sheridan . The movie will draw inspiration from the “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare” games.

“If you really look at the missions and the storylines and the characters like Captain Price, Soap, Ghost and Alex, these are complicated humans. These are not, and no disrespect, cartoon characters or comic books. These are very nuanced storylines; there’s a real soul to the ‘Modern Warfare’ universe. Yes, there’s violence and hardware and equipment and killing. But underneath it, I think the game, and the creators of the game, are really looking at the cost of war, the cost of having to be a warrior who’s, for whatever reason, chosen to put himself between real danger and the rest of us, and the burden that these guys carry.”

Related Stories

'The Odyssey' Artisans Talk Bringing Christopher Nolan's Epic to Life With Practical Sets and Thousands of Costumes at Middleburg Film Fest

Korea Box Office: Anime Feature 'Chiikawa' Edges Past 'The Assassin(s)' to Claim Weekend Crown

Beginning with “Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare” in 2007, the “Modern Warfare” storyline marked the first “Call of Duty” video game to break from the franchise’s original World War II setting. Paramount has yet to reveal any plot details for its upcoming film adaptation, nor has any casting information been made available.

Berg noted at CinemaCon earlier this year that “Taylor and I are both deeply connected to the special ops community” before a sizzle reel highlighted the video game franchise’s continued successes, including 1 billion players and a lifetime revenue of $35 billion.

Paramount announced its “Call of Duty” movie in September 2025. Sources said at the time that while the pact is focused on making one “Call of Duty” movie, the deal included the potential for Paramount to expand the “Call of Duty” universe across film and TV. The movie is currently on Paramount’s release schedule for June 30, 2028.

article_text:
Auch in diesem Jahr bietet die Katholische Akademie Schwerte vom 28. bis 31. Dezember Filmeinkehrtage zum Jahresende an. Das diesjährige Thema „Einsam – zweisam – dreisam?!“ will Teilhabe und Austausch beim gemeinsamen Filmsichten versprechen.

„ Einsam – zweisam – dreisam?!“, lautet das Thema der FilmEinkehrtage zum Jahresende in der Katholischen Akademie Schwerte. Vom 28. bis 31. Dezember bietet sich dort bei der 22. Ausgabe die Gelegenheit, das Jahr im Spiegel von Filmen ausklingen zu lassen.

Der Slogan soll darauf aufmerksam machen, dass Menschen für zwischenmenschliche Beziehungen geschaffen sind. Denn heutzutage leben, besonders in Großstädten, viele Menschen allein und fühlen sich gar einsam. Dem wollen die Einkehrtage mit einer Kombination aus gemeinsamer Filmsichtung und entsprechendem Austausch entgegenwirken.

Die Tage sind so strukturiert, dass genügend Raum zur Verfügung steht, um über Fragen nachzudenken, die von den Filmen angestoßen werden oder die sich aus anderen Zusammenhängen ergeben. Sei es beim Frühstück oder bei Stillarbeiten, im Gruppen- oder im Einzelgespräch. Die Auswahl der abendlichen Filmvorführungen orientiert sich an dem Thema „Einsamkeit“.

Die Filmeinkehrtage richten sich an Menschen ab 18 Jahre, die gerne Filme schauen und sich, der Welt und Gott mithilfe von thematisch ausgewählten Spielfilmen näherkommen möchten. Es ist eine moderne Art, sich alter und doch aktueller Themen gleichermaßen anzunehmen und dabei mit anderen in den Austausch zu kommen. Dazu gehört auch die Bereitschaft, sich aktiv auf das Gespräch mit anderen einzulassen. Eine Offenheit für neuen spirituelle Formen ist nicht fehl am Platz. Denn um neuen Mut zu schöpfen, hilft es meistens, seinen Blickwinkel auf die Dinge zu ändern.

Eine Teilnahme ist allerdings nur am gesamten Kurs möglich, die Teilnehmerzahl ist auf 18 begrenzt; die Filmeinkehrtage enden am 31. Dezember mit einem festlichen Silvesterfrühstück. Begleitet werden die Tage von dem Theologen Thomas Kroll und dem Benediktinermönch Maurus Runge aus der Abteil Königsmünster bei Meschede.

Hinweis

Weitere Information, Programmdetails und Anmeldeformalitäten finden sich auf der Website der Katholischen Akademie Schwerte .

article_text:
Hudson Williams is working on a new film and is “getting tripped up” over a “ Heated Rivalry ” parallel.

Prior to the success of the Canadian queer hockey romance that catapulted the actor to fame over the past year, Williams wrote and directed several short films, including “Soakers,” “Buttons” and “Inside Augustine Mendoza’s Quotidian Apartment.” Now, the actor says he is writing a new project where one character is a former hockey player.

Christy Carlson Romano Says Her Salary Was Half of Shia LaBeouf's on 'Even Stevens': 'We Were Co-Leads and Had the Same Screen Time'

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly for “Yaga,” the Canadian witchy detective-thriller Williams stars in, the actor responded to co-star Carrie-Anne Moss’ hang-up over referencing real-life friend Keanu Reeves’ “John Wick” franchise in the show.

Popular on Variety

“I’m writing a movie right now, but one character is an ex-hockey player,” he said. “We were like, ‘But if we have this hockey player and then you’ve done a hockey show…’ We’re getting tripped up on it and we’re considering other sports, but for some reason this character just made way more sense being an ex-hockey player. It’s almost like you have to bust through the prison of your own mind or construct of your own mind.”

The actor did not elaborate on the nature of the project. It’s far from the only thing Williams is currently or recently working on: “Yaga” premiered on Oct. 23, and production began on the second season of “Heated Rivalry” in August. He will also appear in the dark comedic thriller “Apparatus” opposite Dylan O’Brien, and in the ensemble culinary thriller “Tyrant” with Charlize Theron, Julia Garner, Demi Moore and Omar Apollo.

article_text:
ROOTS & WORLDS 2025: ELSEWHERE, WITHIN

Open studio, 23.11.2025, 16:00-19:00

Showcase 24-30.11.2025, 7:00-19:00

Matca Space for Photography, 48 Ngoc Ha, Ba Đinh, Hanoi

Free entrance

THIS PROGRAM IS MADE POSSIBLE WITH THE CONNECTIONS THROUGH CULTURE GRANT FROM THE BRITISH COUNCIL

THE OPEN STUDIO TAKES PLACE AS PART OF BIENNALE PHOTO HANOI ‘25

Roots & Worlds 2025: Elsewhere, Within is made possible with the Connections Through Culture grant from the British Council. The Open Studio takes place as part of Biennale Photo Hanoi ‘25.

The Open Studio proudly presents six participants, young photographers from different regions across Vietnam, together with the works developed during Roots & Worlds 2025. Six photographers selected through an open call received financial support and artistic mentorship to work on their proposed projects from September to November 2025.

Now in its second iteration, the alternative school for photography returns with the theme Elsewhere, Within. It is co-designed and led by Eugénie Shinkle (University of Westminster, UK) alongside Hà Đào and Linh Phạm (Matca, Vietnam). Roots & Worlds seeks to create an open space for Vietnamese photographers to cultivate their personal voices, using photography as a tool to observe and make sense of their surroundings, and ultimately to situate themselves within the complexity of contemporary life.

The program takes place both online and in person. It begins with a series of online lectures, group discussions, and individual tutorials, followed by a 4-day gathering in Hanoi to collectively edit and present the works.

The Open Studio marks the conclusion of their journey, introducing to the public their discoveries and approaches to a range of topics: the loss of innocence beneath the pressures imposed by school and society; collective identity within public space; the “ritual” of street portraiture and the making of the muse; the sacred within urban life; family history and intergenerational memory; and the transitional space between adolescence and adulthood.

Phan Uyển Nhi is a photographer from Da Nang, now living and studying in Hanoi. For her, photography is a way to observe the world and better understand herself, her family, and her roots.

Inspired by her grandparents’ migration from the North to Central Vietnam after the war, and her own reverse journey to Hanoi, the project explores the quiet inheritances passed across generations. Through staged photographs, archival materials, and everyday images, it reflects on a family history shaped by endurance, tenderness, longing, and the emotional legacy she carries within.

Having lived away from home since the age of thirteen, between the ruptures of inherited values from a small-town childhood and the solitude of city life, Nguyễn Khánh Hoà searches for connections between memory and the present, between the self and its origins, via images and words.

By observing the material forms of and human presence around sacred objects, whether discarded, collected, or entering new afterlives, she traces the intricate weave of cultural and personal beliefs in urban space.

Nguyễn Thanh Hương has a background in fashion and commercial photography. In her personal work, she often blends softness with humor to reflect on the human experience.

Her project examines the seasonal “autumn ritual” of portraiture in Hanoi, where the street becomes a stage and the “muse” a collectively rehearsed aesthetic, further reinforced and circulated through social media. Focusing on moments before the final image: waiting, arranging, and posing, it reveals the deliberate and sometimes awkward process that underlies the seemingly effortless performance of femininity.

Bùi Thị Hoàng Yến is a self-taught artist based in Saigon. Having grown up under societal norms and familial expectations, she turned to art as a sanctuary: a way to resist conformity and reclaim an inner voice that was nearly silenced.

Her project “Vô cùng thương nhớ” (In Loving Memory) traces the loss of innocence as a child’s sense of self buckles under pressure to mold themself into the “good child, good student” model.

Born and raised in Hanoi, Nguyễn Ngọc Phước Vũ began practicing photography in his early high school years. He was drawn to documenting everyday life with his camera or simply with the phone he carried everywhere.

This project marks his own transition from adolescence to adulthood. By revisiting old photographs and keepsakes and placing them into new contexts, while also turning the lens toward himself, Vũ treats the act of looking back as a form of self-exploration: a way to uncover what remains unresolved and to tend to parts of his identity still in the process of healing.

Đinh Hằng Giang, based in Hanoi, is a student with a background in biology and engineering. While her studies taught her how the world functions, she came to photography as a way to inhabit it. Her work focuses on people and the spaces they share.

Her series observes how collective identity takes shape within shared public space, particularly in Thành Công Park (Indira Gandhi Park), a place she has known since childhood. In the park, diverse groups coexist, each expressing themselves through clothing, hairstyles, and accessories, a kind of “social skin” that signals belonging. The project reflects on how these everyday expressions negotiate identity, community, and visibility in an ever-changing urban landscape.

Roots & Worlds is an alternative photography school that combines theory and practice in an intensive three-month program. Through an open call, six emerging Vietnamese photographers will be selected to participate, receiving a production fee and artistic support to develop their projects. It aims to create a space where participants can engage with important ideas and approaches in contemporary photography, while participating in hands-on exercises from conceptualization to production, editing, and presentation.

Roots & Worlds is co-led by Matca, an independent, photographer-run initiative dedicated to opening conversations around photography in Vietnam, with an international partner in photography education. The inaugural edition in 2023 was co-developed by Matca and IC Visual Lab (UK) with the theme Ecological Encounters and supported by the British Council.
